en: The Section on the Yellow and Red [Robes] (Pāṇḍulohitakavastu). Summary of the Contents (Vastūddāna):
The matters of the Pāṇḍulohitakas and likewise of the individuals;
then the parivāsa penance, the suspension of the Poṣadha ceremony, lodgings, legal disputes, and finally, schism in the Saṃgha.
Pāṇḍ-v § 0.2 // Summary Verse (uddāna) of the Pāṇḍulohitaka-vastu //
For the Pāṇḍulohitakas there was the tarjanīya [action], and for Śreyaka the nigarhaṇīya;
for Aśvaka and Punarvasuka there was the pravāsa, which Uttara subsequently rescinded.
This refers to non-seeing, as well as non-restitution of the *chanda*;
it is the view of one who has committed a grave offense (*ariṣṭa-pāpīya*), and [it concerns] Udāyin’s fivefold action.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.

Now at that time, there lived in Śrāvastī certain monks who were pale-red (pāṇḍulohitaka), who were makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and creators of legal issues.
They frequently gave rise to legal issues within the Saṅgha, by which the Saṅgha dwelt having become embroiled in strife, embroiled in quarrels, divided, and fallen into dispute.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you must carry out the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) against the monks Pāṇḍulohitaka, who are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, contentious, fallen into dispute, and litigants."
Regarding "the act" (*karma*): furthermore,
whatever other [act] of this same kind there may be—

when the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*) is performed for five reasons, that is an illegal act (*adharmakarman*) and an act not in accordance with the discipline (*avinayakarman*), and because of it, the Saṃgha incurs an offense (*sātisāra*).
By which five?
They perform it without having accused [the person], without having reminded [them], without a factual basis, without a formal admission, and they perform it against one who is not present.

However, when the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) is performed for five reasons, it is a legal act (*dharmakarma*), it is an act of discipline (*vinayakarma*), and the Saṃgha is thereby not at fault.
By which five [methods]?
They act after having reproached [the offender], after having reminded [them], with a factual basis, by means of a formal admission, and in the presence of the person concerned.
And furthermore, it should be performed in this manner: [Pāṇḍ-v § 1.3]

Having prepared the seats and bedding, struck the ghaṇṭā, and questioned the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has sat down and assembled, one monk should make a formal motion (*jñapti*) and perform the ritual act (*karman*).
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha! [Pāṇḍ-v § 1.4]
These Pāṇḍulohitaka monks are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and creators of legal issues.
They frequently give rise to legal issues within the Saṃgha, by which the Saṃgha dwells having become embroiled in strife, embroiled in quarrels, divided, and fallen into dispute.
If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, if it so approves, [grant] that the Saṃgha [perform] for the Pāṇḍulohitakas...

"Let the formal motion be made: 'The act of censure should be performed against those monks who cause strife, who cause quarrels, who cause disputes, who cause contention, and who instigate legal cases. This is the motion.
Then the formal act (karman) should be performed:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
These monks, the Pāṇḍulohitakas, are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and creators of legal issues."
These very individuals frequently give rise to legal disputes within the Saṃgha, by which the Saṃgha dwells embroiled in quarrels, embroiled in strife, contentious, and fallen into dispute.

Therefore, the Saṃgha performs the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) against these Pāṇḍulohitaka monks—those who create quarrels, those who create strife, those who create discord, those who create disputes, and those who instigate legal disputes.

"Those venerable ones for whom it is acceptable to carry out the act of censure against the monks Pāṇḍulohitaka—as previously described—should remain silent; those for whom it is not acceptable should speak.
This is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*);
the second and third proclamations should be performed in the same manner."

The Saṃgha has performed the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) against the monks Pāṇḍulohitaka, as previously described, up to [the point of] the formal act. Since the Saṃgha is silent, this is accepted and authorized; thus do I hold it to be so. Pāṇ-v § 1.6: I shall prescribe the rules of customary conduct for a monk against whom the act of censure has been performed. A monk against whom the act of censure has been performed must not grant the going-forth (*pravrajyā*).
One should not grant full ordination; one should not provide formal dependence;
one should not admit a novice monk;
and one should not instruct a nun.
A monk should not be appointed as an instructor of nuns, nor should a nun be instructed by one who has already been so appointed.
Furthermore, a monk should not be accused or reminded of a failure in morality, a failure in view, a failure in conduct, or a failure in livelihood; he should not be formally censured for these.
There is no *poṣadha*, no *pravāraṇā*, no formal act consisting of a motion (*jñapti-karman*), nor a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*).
A monk against whom the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) has been performed who does not undertake and abide by the rules of customary conduct as they have been prescribed incurs an offense.
Pāṇḍ-v § 1.7: Those against whom the act of censure has been performed thus, with hair bristling upward and outward, cause their body hairs to stand on end within the Saṃgha.
They set forth the means of deliverance, demonstrate proper conduct, remain within the boundary, request reinstatement, and say, "We shall desist from being quarrelsome.
The monks report this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One says:
"Monks, you should reinstate the monks Paṇḍulohitaka, who were makers of strife and against whom the act of censure was performed," or whoever else is of a similar kind.
Pāṇ-v § 1.8a: One against whom the act of censure has been performed and who is endowed with five qualities should not be reinstated.
With which five?
He tears out his hair and the hair of others before the Saṃgha; he does not initiate the formal act of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*); he does not demonstrate proper conduct (*sāmīcī*);
he does not stand within the boundary (*antaḥsīmā*) and request reinstatement (*osāraṇā*); and because of his quarrelsome nature, he says, "I do not desist from this.
Endowed with these five qualities, [the procedure is] as stated previously.
Furthermore, one who has been subjected to the act of censure (tarjanīyakarman) should not be removed [from his position] even if he possesses five other qualities.
What are these five?
He relies upon royal families, he relies upon official families, he relies upon non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthika), he relies upon individuals, and he does not rely upon the Saṃgha.
Endowed with these five qualities, as previously stated, [he is not to be removed].
Furthermore, one who has undergone the act of censure (tarjanīyakarman) is not to be removed if he is endowed with another five qualities.
What are these five?

He bears the banner of a householder, he bears the banner of a non-Buddhist, he serves, frequents, and attends upon non-Buddhists, he practices improper conduct, and he does not train in the training of a monk.
Endowed with these five qualities, as previously stated, [he is subject to the act of censure].
Furthermore, one who has been subjected to the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) should not be removed from his status if he is endowed with another five qualities.
By which five?
He reviles, enrages, and insults monks; and he intends for the sake of the Saṅgha’s lack of gain and its decline.
By these five factors, as previously stated.
However, one who has undergone the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*) is to be reinstated (*osārayitavya*) when endowed with five qualities.
With which five qualities?

He tears out his hair and plucks out the hair on his body before the Saṃgha; he sets forth the means of deliverance; he demonstrates proper conduct; and, standing within the boundary (*antaḥsīmā*), he requests reinstatement.

And if one says, "I shall abstain from being a cause of quarrel," then one who has been subjected to the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*) and is endowed with these five qualities should be reinstated. Furthermore, one who has been subjected to the act of censure and is endowed with another five qualities should also be reinstated.
By which five?
He does not rely on the royal family, he does not rely on the official class, he does not rely on non-Buddhist teachers, he relies on the Saṅgha, and he does not rely on an individual.
Endowed with these five qualities, it is as stated previously.
Pāṇḍ-v § 1.9c: One who has undergone the act of censure (tarjanīyakarman) may be reinstated when endowed with five other qualities.
With which five?

He does not bear the banner of a householder, nor does he bear the banner of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika); he does not serve, associate with, or attend upon non-Buddhists; he practices superior conduct and trains in the training of a monk.
As before, by these five qualities;
furthermore, one who has undergone the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*) is to be reinstated when endowed with another five qualities.
What are those five?
He does not revile the monks, does not incense them, and does not reproach them; he intends for the gain of the Saṃgha and not for its dejection.
By these five qualities, as previously stated.
*Pāṇḍ-v* § 1.10 And furthermore, he is to be reinstated in this manner:

Having prepared the seats and bedding, struck the ghaṇṭā, and exhorted the monks by means of an inquiry, when the entire Saṅgha has sat down and assembled, the Pāṇḍulohitaka monks, having performed the proper salutation according to seniority, should stand in a crouching position at the end of the elders, join their palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
We, the monks Pāṇḍulohitaka, are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and creators of legal issues.
We repeatedly give rise to legal issues within the Saṃgha, by which the Saṃgha dwells having become embroiled in strife, embroiled in quarrels, divided, and fallen into dispute."

The Saṃgha has performed the act of censure against us, the Pāṇḍulohitaka monks— who were makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention, and instigators of legal cases.
Having been subjected to the act of censure, we, with our hair bristling and disheveled, cause hairs to fall upon the Saṃgha and proclaim our renunciation.
We demonstrate our proper conduct; standing within the boundary, we request reinstatement. And we desist from being quarrelsome.

May the venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, take pity upon us—the monks Pāṇḍulohitaka—who were quarrelsome, contentious, creators of legal disputes, and who have undergone the act of censure, and reinstate us.
Thus a second and a third time.
Thereafter, one monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen."

These Pāṇḍulohitaka monks are quarrelsome and, moreover, litigious; they repeatedly give rise to legal disputes within the Saṃgha, by which the Saṃgha dwells embroiled in strife, quarreling, contentious, and fallen into dispute. Therefore, the Saṃgha has performed the act of censure against them for being quarrelsome.

These very monks, who were subjected to the act of censure, now have their hair standing on end and disheveled; they shed tears before the Saṃgha, they declare their desire for deliverance, they demonstrate proper conduct, and standing within the boundary, they request reinstatement. They say, "We shall desist from being quarrelsome. If it seems the proper time to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its permission that the Saṃgha reinstate the monks Pāṇḍula and Lohitaka.
He brings about the departure [from the offense].
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Thereafter, the ritual act (*karman*) should be performed.
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. These monks, the Pāṇḍulohitakas, are quarrelsome, and so forth, up to being litigants."

These individuals frequently incite legal disputes within the Saṃgha, by which the Saṃgha dwells embroiled in quarrels, engaged in strife, divided, and fallen into contention. Therefore, the Saṃgha has performed the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) against them as "quarrel-makers. Having been subjected to this act of censure, they now—with hair bristling and disheveled—cause their body hairs to fall upon the Saṃgha, propose an escape from their status, and demonstrate proper conduct; standing within the boundary (*sīmā*), they seek reinstatement (*osāraṇā*).
They beg [for forgiveness],
saying, "We shall desist from being quarrelsome. Therefore, the Saṃgha reinstates the Pāṇḍulohitaka monks who were makers of strife and had been subjected to the act of censure (tarjanīyakarman).
Those venerable ones who approve of reinstating the monks Pāṇḍulohitaka—who were quarrelsome and had been subjected to the act of censure—should remain silent; those who do not approve should speak.
The monks Pāṇḍulohitaka, who were quarrelsome and had been subjected to the act of censure, have been reinstated by the Saṃgha.
Since there is silence, it is understood that the Saṃgha has approved; thus do I hold this to be so.
Pāṇḍ-v § 2.1: The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
At that time, there was a monk named Śreyaka who was a frequent offender; he repeatedly committed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
While the monks were granting him *parivāsa*, they also granted him *mūlaparivāsa* and *mānāpya*, and were carrying out his *āvarhaṇa*.
They have many duties and much to do; they neglect the oral instruction, the recitation, the private study, the practice of yoga, the mental attention, and the internal tranquility of mind.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, perform the act of censure against the monk Śreyaka for his repeated offenses;
or whoever else is of such a kind."

Pāṇḍ-v § 2.2a: A formal act of censure (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*) performed for five reasons is both non-Dharma and contrary to Dharma, it is a non-discipline (*avinaya-karman*), and because of it, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.

What are the five? They perform it without having charged [the accused]; they perform it without having reminded [him]; they perform it without a factual basis; they perform it without a confession; and they perform it against one who is not present.

But when a formal act of censure (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*) is performed for five reasons, it is a legal act (*dharma-karman*) and a disciplinary act (*vinaya-karman*), and the Saṃgha is not at fault because of it.
What are these five?

They perform it after having reproached [the offender], having reminded [him of his offense], having established the factual basis, having obtained a confession, and while the person is present in person.
And furthermore, it should be performed in this manner:

having prepared the seating and bedding, struck the ghaṇṭī, and exhorted the monks by means of an inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has sat down and assembled, one monk should make a formal motion (*jñapti*) and the ritual act (*karman*) should be performed.
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
This monk Śreyaka is one who repeatedly commits offenses; he repeatedly incurs *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Therefore, while the monks are granting him *parivāsa*, *mūlaparivāsa*, *mānāpya*, and performing the *āvarhaṇa*, they have many duties."
They have many duties to perform and thus neglect the recitation, the reading, the private study, the practice of yoga, the mental application, and the internal tranquility of mind.

If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha, if it so consents, authorize that the Saṃgha perform a formal act of censure (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*) against the monk Śreyaka for his repeated offenses. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
And the formal act should be performed in this manner: [Pāṇḍ-v § 2.5]
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
This monk Śreyaka is one who repeatedly commits offenses; he repeatedly incurs *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Therefore, while the monks are granting him *parivāsa*, *mūlaparivāsa*, *mānāpya*, and *āvarhaṇa*, they are occupied with many duties."
They have many duties to perform and thus neglect the recitation, the study, the private recitation, the practice of yoga, the mental attention, and the internal tranquility of mind.
Therefore, the Saṃgha performs a formal act of censure against the monk Śreyaka for his repeated offenses.
For those venerable ones who consent to the formal act of censure against Śreyaka— [290v1 = GBM 893]
If you do not consent in silence to perform the act of censure against this monk who repeatedly commits offenses, speak up;
this is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*). The second and third formal proclamations should be performed in the same manner.
The Saṃgha has performed the act of censure against the monk Śreyaka for his repeated offenses.
The Saṃgha has consented and authorized this, since it is silent; thus do I understand this to be so.
I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk against whom the act of censure has been carried out.
A monk against whom the act of censure has been carried out must not grant the going-forth,
nor must he grant full ordination.
No dependence shall be granted;
no novice shall be ordained. As previously stated, this applies up to the case of one against whom the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*) has been performed.

A monk against whom the act of reprimand (*nigarhaṇīyakarman*) has been performed who does not undertake and abide by the prescribed rules of conduct (*āsamudācārikadharma*) incurs an offense of transgression.

Having been subjected to the act of censure (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*) in this manner, he, with his hair bristling and disheveled, sheds tears before the Saṃgha as previously described, up until standing within the boundary (*antaḥsīmā*) and requesting reinstatement (*osāraṇā*).
He declares, "I shall desist from repeated offenses.
The monks report this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, you should reinstate the monk Śreyaka who has undergone the *nigarhaṇīyakarman* (act of censure), or whoever else is of a similar nature.
One who has undergone the *nigarhaṇīyakarman* and is endowed with five qualities should be reinstated."

By which five [acts]? He tears out his hair and plucks out the hair on his body before the Saṃgha; he proclaims his renunciation; he demonstrates proper conduct; standing within the boundary, he requests reinstatement; and he says, "I shall desist from being a habitual offender."
And furthermore, it should be restored in this manner:

having prepared the seating arrangements, struck the ghaṇṭī, and exhorted the monks with a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha is seated and assembled, the monk Śreyaka should stand crouching at the end of the row of elders and, raising his joined palms, [speak as follows].
This should be said:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen.
I, the monk Śreyaka, am one who repeatedly commits offenses; I repeatedly incur *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses."

"Monks, while granting me probation, the *mūlaparivāsa*, the *mānāpya*, and the *āvarhaṇa*, they have become burdened with many duties and many tasks; they neglect the recitation, the reading, the study, the practice, the mental attention, and the internal tranquility of mind. The Saṃgha has performed a formal act of censure against me."
Thus, having been subjected to the act of censure (nigarhaṇīyakarman), with my hair standing on end and disheveled, I cast down my body-hair before the Saṅgha;
I proclaim my renunciation, I demonstrate proper conduct, and staying within the boundary, I beg for reinstatement.
"And because of my habitual committing of offenses, I shall desist from them.
May the venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, restore me, the monk Śreyaka, who has committed habitual offenses and for whom the act of censure has been performed.
Thus he says a second and a third time.
Thereafter, a single monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*):
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
This monk Śreyaka is one who repeatedly commits offenses... [as before] ...up to internal tranquility of mind."
The Saṃgha has performed a *nigarhaṇīya-karman* (act of censure) against him for being a habitual offender; [the motion] is that he should be reinstated.
And the act is to be performed as follows:

Having been subjected to the *nigarhaṇīya-karman*, with his hair disheveled and his locks flying, he sheds tears before the Saṃgha, as previously described, up until: "because of being a habitual offender..."

And he says, "I shall desist. If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha, if it so approves, authorize that the Saṃgha should rehabilitate the monk Śreyaka, who has repeatedly committed offenses and for whom the act of censure has been performed; this is the motion (*jñapti*).
And the formal act (*karman*) should be carried out in this manner.
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
Venerable sirs, this monk Śreyaka is one who repeatedly commits offenses; he repeatedly incurs *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
Venerable sirs, let the monks grant him *parivāsa*, as before, up until [he attains] internal tranquility of mind."

The Saṃgha has performed a *nigarhaṇīya-karman* (act of censure) against this monk Śreyaka for being a habitual offender. This very monk Śreyaka, having been subjected to the *nigarhaṇīya-karman* for being a habitual offender, now— with hair standing on end and hair disheveled— causes his body hair to fall before the Saṃgha, demonstrates the means of deliverance, displays proper decorum, and, remaining within the boundary (*sīmā*), requests reinstatement because of his status as a habitual offender.
And he says, "I shall desist.

Therefore, the Saṃgha restores the monk Śreyaka, who was repeatedly committing offenses and for whom the act of censure had been performed. Those venerable ones who consent to restoring the monk Śreyaka, who was repeatedly committing offenses and for whom the act of censure had been performed, [should remain silent].
Since they remain silent, they do not object; let them speak.
This is the first formal proclamation (karmavācanā); in this same manner, the second and third formal proclamations are to be performed.
The monk Śreyaka, who was repeatedly committing offenses and had been subjected to the *nigarhaṇīya-karman* by the Saṃgha, has been reinstated by the Saṃgha.
Since the Saṃgha has consented and authorized this by remaining silent, I shall hold it to be so.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
Now at that time, two monks from Kiṭāgiri, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, were residing there; they were corrupters of families and practitioners of evil conduct.
These two perform and cause others to perform such un-monastic deeds as these:

namely, they laugh together with women, play together, and engage in boisterous chatter; they display restlessness, frivolity, and physical agitation; and even now, they sit upon the same seat and eat from the same row.
They drink various kinds of intoxicants through single-stemmed vessels;
they pluck flowers,
gather them, weave garlands, and have them woven.
They were binding garlands, causing others to bind them;
dancing, causing others to dance; singing, causing others to sing.
Engaging in debate and causing others to debate; bestowing rewards for excellent dancing, singing, and instrumental music;
and gathering up their robes to run, rush, and hasten away.
They also perform the turning of the thighs and the turning of the arms; they also perform the whirlpool of the Rohita fish; and they pierce with a water-sieve.
They even played the water-machines and the water-drums; they even trumpeted like elephants and cranes, neighed like horses,
and bellowed like bulls.
They even play the face-drum;
they blow the face-conch and beat the face-drum; they even utter the cry of a peacock, and they even warble the song of a cuckoo.
They engage in elephant fights; they engage in horse fights, bull fights, buffalo fights, goat fights, ball fights, women’s fights,
men’s fights, boys’ fights, girls’ fights, cock fights, quail fights, and partridge fights, or cause them to be engaged in.
They perform these and other deeds unworthy of a śramaṇa, and cause others to do so.
Because of their manner of conduct, behavior, and practice, monks who have not yet come to Kiṭāgiri do not come;
and those who have already come find no delight and abandon their residence at Kiṭāgiri.
The brahmins and householders residing on Mount Kiṭa were neither pleased nor satisfied;
they considered it a hardship even to provide alms-food to the local residents who had long been with them,
let alone to those who were newcomers.
Then, at another time, the venerable Ānanda, while wandering on a tour through the Kāśī country,
arrived at Kiṭāgiri and stayed there at the Kiṭāgiri forest grove.
Then the venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kiṭāgiri for alms.

Just as he had entered Kiṭāgiri for alms with a clean bowl, so too did he depart with that same clean bowl, having received neither an offering nor a refusal, not even so much as a single morsel of alms-food.
Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
"In the past, this Kiṭāgiri was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people and inhabitants, and alms-food was easily obtained by beggars;
even now, this Kiṭāgiri is prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants."
Moreover, just as I entered with my bowl washed, so too did I depart with my bowl washed, having received neither an offering nor a refusal, not even so much as a single morsel of alms.

May it not be that some foolish, unrefined, or unskilled disciple of the Blessed One, under the influence of the afflictions, has here addressed, touched, or reviled a woman of good family or a maiden of good family.

At that time, about five hundred brahmins and householders from Kiṭāgiri were seated and assembled in their assembly hall for some particular business. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the assembly hall of the brahmins and householders from Kiṭāgiri.
Having approached, he said this to the brahmins and householders of Kiṭāgiri:
"Sirs, formerly this Kiṭāgiri was as it was described before, until [the point where] not even a single alms-meal was obtained.
When this was said, the brahmins and householders of Kiṭāgiri stood with their senses cast down.
At that time, the lay follower Udakaplotika was seated and present in that very assembly.
Then the lay follower Udakaplotika took the arm of the Venerable Ānanda, stepped aside to one side, and said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Venerable Ānanda, you should know that on this Mount Kiṭā there dwell two monks, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, who are corrupters of families and practitioners of evil conduct; they [dwell] together with women."
[They] laughed together, as before, up to [the point where it says]:

"Venerable Ānanda, as before, up to [the point where it says]: 'Just as in the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule concerning the corrupter of families (*kuladūṣaka*), perform the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against the two monks Aśvaka and Punarvasuka.
(Pāṇḍ-v § 3.5) And furthermore, it should be performed in this manner: (Pāṇḍ-v § 3.6)
A monk who acts as a proponent (*codaka*) should be appointed while standing on the path inside.
A monk who acts as a proponent must be endowed with five qualities, as previously described, up until the point where they perform the formal act (*karman*).
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!... (Pāṇḍ-v § 3.7)
These two monks, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, are corrupters of families and practitioners of evil dharmas.
It is seen, heard, and known that families have been corrupted by them;
their evil conduct is also seen, heard, and known.
